newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark to encourage access to mezzanine capital.
newsitem.headline: Denmark to encourage access to mezzanine capital.

text.p: Trade and Industry Minister Mimi Jakobsen pledged on Thursday to boost mezzanine capital flows in Denmark by promoting a market in such second tier debt.

She was speaking at a Confederation of Danish Industries (DI) small business conference, where delegates asked for help in gaining access to mezzanine capital -- a high-yielding form of debt which is not as secure as senior debt.
"Here we agree completely with DI. We are in fact already working on initiatives to support development of a market for mezzanine capital," she said.

"Far too many new Danish businesses go bankrupt early on. Many of them could perhaps have been saved had they not needed to pay banks' high rates of interest," Jakobsen said, implying they could instead turn to mezzanine finance, which could be linked to equity values.
She said that the government planned eight new initiatives next year under the umbrella of "more and cheaper capital", most of them aimed at helping small and medium-sized businesses.
Among them, she said, was planned legislation to give Danish investment associations the right to offer the same range of products as their foreign counterparts.
Another goal was to encourage pension funds to place more resources in small and medium-sized businesses.

"A new bill will make it possible that part of pension institutes' resources can be placed in business development associations, which are a new kind of investment association which will invest in unlisted shares," Jakobsen said.
She added that her ministry was considering extending the life of its programme to provide venture capital and advice and would give tax incentives for development of new ideas.

"And in concrete terms we shall encourage mezzanine capital by promoting the lending of subordinated loans through private institutions. The trade industry wants to get a market for subordinated loans started," she said.
DI Chairman Svend-Aage Nielsen said that mezzanine capital had a number of advantages for both industry and investors.

"Access to mezzanine capital will create possibilities to initiate activities that would not otherwise be realised. A relatively low basic rate of interest will make it attractive for businesses to borrow, while the additional interest element will reflect the return on investments," he said.

"And in the final analysis firms will not have to surrender sovereignty as they would when issuing voting shares," Nielsen said, adding that the government had budgeted 20 million crowns ($3.3 million) to stimulate loan flows to smaller businesses.

"Use those 20 million crowns as a project grant for an existing financial player -- after a tender -- whose assignment would be to create the necessary infrastructure for mezzanine capital and with it, the foundations of a market for this form of capital," Nielsen said.
"DI has shown the way with a finished concept, now the ball is in the politicians' court," he said.
